claims.text: High-entropy nanoalloys have enhanced structural stability at high temperatures.
A stable disordered phase is responsible for the enhanced high-temperature structural stability.
The stable disordered phase minimizes atomic mobility.
The high-entropy nanoalloys initially have a homogeneous disordered state at room temperature.
The disordered phase stabilizes the atomic arrangement.
The disordered phase reduces the energy barrier for atomic rearrangement.
Reducing the energy barrier for atomic rearrangement maintains structural integrity under thermal stress.
At the same high-temperature conditions, high-entropy nanoalloys will exhibit less phase separation than lower-entropy alloys.
At the same high-temperature conditions, high-entropy nanoalloys will retain a more uniform structure than lower-entropy alloys.
Lower-entropy alloys are expected to undergo significant phase separation at high temperatures.
Lower-entropy alloys are expected to undergo significant structural degradation at high temperatures.
The prediction applies to high-entropy nanoalloys at temperatures up to 1000°C.
Above 1000°C, degradation mechanisms other than loss of disorder-mediated stability may dominate.
Heating high- and lower-entropy alloys under identical conditions and measuring phase separation can test the prediction.
Greater phase separation and structural degradation in the high-entropy nanoalloys than in the lower-entropy controls would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes stability to minimized atomic mobility, whereas the mechanism says the disordered phase lowers the barrier for atomic rearrangement. A lower rearrangement barrier would ordinarily facilitate, rather than suppress, rearrangement, so the proposed causal direction is internally inconsistent.
